title: Real Estate LLC vs Sole Proprietorship: Which Is Better for Investors?
excerpt: Choosing between a real estate LLC and sole proprietorship is one of the most important decisions you'll make as an investor. This guide breaks down the pros, cons, taxes, and liability differences so you can pick the right structure for your business.

sections.content: When you close your first real estate deal, business structure might be the last thing on your mind. But choosing between a real estate LLC vs sole proprietorship — which is better for your situation — is a decision that affects your taxes, your personal assets, and your ability to grow. Get it wrong and you could face a lawsuit that wipes out your savings. Get it right and you'll have a foundation that supports real, scalable growth. If you're working toward building a serious investing operation, check out the [Scaling a Real Estate Investing Business: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/scaling-real-estate-investing-business) — it covers everything from your first deal to running a full team. This article focuses on the business structure decision specifically, with real numbers and clear guidance to help you choose.
What Is a Sole Proprietorship in Real Estate?

A sole proprietorship is the default business structure. If you buy and sell a property without registering a formal business entity, you are automatically operating as a sole proprietor. There's no paperwork to file, no registration fee, and no separation between you and your business. Your profits show up on your personal tax return (Schedule C), and you pay self-employment tax on them — currently 15.3% on the first $160,200 of net income. For a new investor closing one or two deals a year, this simplicity can feel like an advantage. But that simplicity comes with a serious downside: unlimited personal liability.
What Is an LLC and How Does It Work for Real Estate?

A Limited Liability Company (LLC) is a legal entity that separates your personal finances from your business. If a tenant sues your LLC because they slipped and fell on your rental property, your personal bank account, home, and car are generally protected — the lawsuit can only go after assets owned by the LLC. Single-member LLCs are taxed the same as sole proprietorships by default (pass-through taxation), but you gain that critical liability shield. Multi-member LLCs are taxed like partnerships. Either way, you can also elect to be taxed as an S-Corp once your income reaches a certain threshold, which can save you thousands in self-employment taxes each year.
Side-by-Side Comparison: LLC vs Sole Proprietorship

items: Liability Protection — LLC wins. Sole proprietors have zero protection. One lawsuit can cost you everything personally.
Startup Cost — Sole proprietorship wins. It costs nothing to start. LLCs typically cost $50–$500 to register depending on the state.
Annual Maintenance — Sole proprietorship wins. LLCs require annual reports and fees ranging from $25 in Kentucky to $800 in California.
Tax Flexibility — LLC wins. You can elect S-Corp status and reduce self-employment taxes once you're earning over roughly $40,000–$50,000 in net profit.
Credibility — LLC wins. Buyers, sellers, and lenders take 'Smith Properties LLC' more seriously than just your name.
Privacy — LLC wins. In most states, your LLC keeps your personal name off public property records.
Financing — LLC can complicate things. Some lenders won't offer conventional loans to LLCs, requiring portfolio or commercial loans instead.

sections.content: The Tax Math That Actually Matters

Let's use a concrete example. Say you're wholesaling real estate and you net $80,000 in assignment fees this year. As a sole proprietor, you pay 15.3% self-employment tax on that full amount — roughly $12,240 — on top of your income tax. If your LLC elects S-Corp status, you pay yourself a reasonable salary of, say, $45,000. You pay payroll taxes only on that salary (about $6,885). The remaining $35,000 passes through as a distribution — no self-employment tax. That's a savings of over $5,000 in one year, enough to cover your LLC costs many times over. As you scale toward [closing 10 deals per month](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/scaling-wholesale-deals-per-month), these savings compound fast.

Pro Tip: The S-Corp election generally makes sense once your LLC nets $40,000 or more per year. Below that threshold, the accounting and payroll costs may cancel out the tax savings. Talk to a CPA who works specifically with real estate investors before making this move.
When a Sole Proprietorship Actually Makes Sense

There are legitimate situations where starting as a sole proprietor is reasonable — but they're narrow. If you are testing the waters with your very first deal, you have no significant personal assets to protect, and you're in a state where LLC fees are high (looking at you, California at $800/year), delaying your LLC formation for 60–90 days while you close that first deal is not catastrophic. Many successful investors did exactly this. The key is treating it as a temporary situation, not a permanent strategy. If you're reading a [real estate investing beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) and just getting started, know that forming your LLC should be one of your first 10 action items — not an afterthought.

'The cost of forming an LLC is trivial compared to the cost of a single lawsuit. I've seen investors lose their personal home over a tenant dispute that could have been completely avoided with a $150 LLC registration.' — Common advice from real estate attorneys who work with investors
How to Set Up an LLC for Real Estate: Step-by-Step
Step 1: Choose Your State

Most investors should form their LLC in the state where they do business. Forming in Delaware or Wyoming for tax benefits sounds appealing but usually adds complexity and cost for small operators. If you're investing in active markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), or [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), just form your LLC in that state to keep things simple.
Step 2: File Your Articles of Organization

Visit your state's Secretary of State website and file your Articles of Organization. You'll need a name (check availability), a registered agent address (this can be a service like Northwest Registered Agent for about $39/year), and the filing fee. This typically takes 1–3 business days online.
Step 3: Get an EIN and Open a Business Bank Account

Apply for a free Employer Identification Number (EIN) at IRS.gov — it takes about 10 minutes. Then open a dedicated business bank account. This is non-negotiable. Mixing personal and business funds (called 'piercing the corporate veil') can eliminate your liability protection entirely.
Step 4: Create an Operating Agreement

Even as a single-member LLC, draft an operating agreement. This document outlines how the business runs, who owns what, and how decisions are made. Many states require it, and it's critical evidence that your LLC is a real, separate business entity.
Should You Use One LLC or Multiple?

As your portfolio grows, experienced investors often use multiple LLCs — one per property or one per strategy. For example, your wholesale operation runs through one LLC, while your rental portfolio lives in another. This way, a lawsuit on a rental property can't touch your wholesale business assets. If you're thinking about [bringing on an acquisitions manager](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/acquisitions-manager-real-estate) or building out a team, having a separate operating LLC for your business and a holding LLC for assets is a common structure attorneys recommend. The tradeoff is more administrative overhead and multiple sets of annual fees.

Pro Tip: Before you move properties into an LLC, check with your lender. Many mortgage agreements include a 'due-on-sale' clause that could be triggered by transferring title — even to your own LLC. This is especially important for properties with existing conventional mortgages.
Run Your Deal Numbers Before Worrying About Structure

Business structure matters, but it won't save a bad deal. Before you get wrapped up in entity formation, make sure every deal you evaluate makes financial sense. Use the free [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) at AIWholesail to quickly run your numbers — including MAO (maximum allowable offer), estimated profit, and repair costs — before you ever make an offer. Strong deal analysis is the foundation of a profitable investing business, whether you're operating as a sole proprietor today or running three LLCs tomorrow. Once your deals are consistent, also think about your [disposition strategies](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/wholesale-disposition-strategies) to move properties faster and keep cash flowing.
The Bottom Line: Which Is Better?

For most real estate investors — whether you're wholesaling, flipping, or building a rental portfolio — an LLC is the better choice. The liability protection alone justifies the cost. If you're brand new and closing your very first deal, a brief stint as a sole proprietor isn't the end of the world, but it should be temporary. Form your LLC as soon as your business is real and consistent. As your income grows, talk to a CPA about the S-Corp election for additional tax savings. If you're new to the business and want to understand the full picture before forming your entity, the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) is a great starting point.
